# The Sky Above Us

Before you read on, a question. Tonight, from where you live, where is
Polaris, the North Star? Straight overhead? On the horizon? Somewhere in
between? Commit to an answer. We will come back to it.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- describe the sky as a sphere centered on you, and name its landmarks;
- explain why the Sun and stars rise and set, and which stars never set;
- measure angles on the sky with your hand.

## The Celestial Sphere {#the-celestial-sphere}

Stand outside on a clear night and the sky looks like a dome, with the stars
painted on the inside. Astronomers keep that picture and complete it into a
full sphere with you at the center: the **celestial sphere**.

It is a model, not a real shell. The stars are at wildly different distances.
But the model tells you exactly where to look, and that is what we want from
it. Think of an open umbrella over your head with stars painted on the inside.

Four landmarks on the sphere matter:

- **Zenith**: the point straight over your head.
- **Horizon**: the circle where the sky meets the ground.
- **Celestial poles**: where Earth's axis, extended into space, meets the
  sphere. The north celestial pole is very close to Polaris.
- **Celestial equator**: Earth's equator projected onto the sky, halfway
  between the poles.

Point at each one with your arm. Your body is a better diagram than this page.

## Why the Sky Turns {#daily-motion}

Earth spins from west to east once a day. From the ground, that makes the
whole sky appear to turn from east to west around the celestial poles, about
15 degrees every hour (360 degrees in 24 hours).

Spin slowly in an office chair and the room goes around you. Nothing in the
room moved. The Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars all rise in the east
and set in the west for that one reason.

Now the answer to the opening question. Polaris sits almost exactly at the
north celestial pole, so it barely moves all night. Its height above your
northern horizon, its **altitude**, equals your latitude. From 45 degrees
north it is halfway up the sky. From the equator it sits on the horizon. From
the North Pole it is straight overhead.

Stars closer to the pole than your latitude circle it without ever setting.
These are the **circumpolar stars**. From 45 degrees north, the Big Dipper is
circumpolar: it is up all night, every night of the year.

## Measuring Angles With Your Hand {#measuring-angles}

We cannot tell how far away a star is by looking at it, so positions on the
sky are angles, not lengths. Your hand, held at arm's length, is a surprisingly
good protractor:

| Hand at arm's length | Angle |
|---|---|
| Little finger | about 1 degree |
| Three middle fingers | about 5 degrees |
| Closed fist | about 10 degrees |
| Spread hand, thumb to little finger | about 20 degrees |

The full Moon is only half a degree across. It hides behind your little
finger, which surprises almost everyone.

For smaller angles, a degree splits into 60 **arcminutes**, and an arcminute
into 60 **arcseconds**, the same pattern as hours, minutes and seconds. So one
degree is 3,600 arcseconds. Remember the arcsecond: in AST 102 it is how we
measure the distance to the stars.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it tonight"}
Find the Big Dipper. The two stars at the end of its bowl, the pointers, are
about half a fist apart, so about 5 degrees. Follow the line they make for
about five times that distance and you reach Polaris. Measure its altitude in
fists and compare with your latitude. Put it in your observing log.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="c">
  <div class="question">1. You live at latitude 30 degrees north. Where is Polaris?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> At the zenith</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> On the northern horizon</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> Due north, 30 degrees above the horizon</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> It moves across the sky during the night</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>c</strong>. The altitude of Polaris equals your latitude. It stays put because it sits almost exactly at the celestial pole.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="b">
  <div class="question">2. Two stars look three fingers apart at arm's length. About how far apart are they in arcminutes?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> 5</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> 300</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> 3,600</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> 18,000</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>b</strong>. Three fingers is about 5 degrees, and each degree is 60 arcminutes.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

Daily motion comes back in every chapter of AST 101: the Moon's rising time
in the next chapter, the Sun's path in the seasons. The arcsecond comes back
in AST 102, when we measure how far away the stars are.
